summary: Proposes RA-Guard, a lightweight way to block unwanted IPv6 Router Advertisements by filtering in the layer-2 network fabric, as an alternative or complement to Secure Neighbor Discovery. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RA-Guard lets a network switch check IPv6 router announcements and block ones that do not meet its rules. It only protects a network when the relevant traffic passes through devices that enforce those rules.

questions: how to block rogue router advertisements
does ra guard work with send
subtitle: A layer-2 switch can filter IPv6 router announcements before they reach hosts.

tldr.problem: An unauthorized or misconfigured router can send IPv6 Router Advertisements on a shared layer-2 segment. Secure Neighbor Discovery can address this, but the RFC describes it as difficult to deploy completely.
tldr.mechanism: RA-Guard has a layer-2 device inspect incoming advertisements and forward or block them using configured rules, learned senders, or SEND validation.
tldr.outcome: RA-Guard complements SEND, but cannot protect traffic that bypasses controlled layer-2 devices or travels through IPv6 tunnels. RFC 6105 was updated by RFC 7113.

today: RFC 6105 is an Informational document updated by RFC 7113. Its protection applies only where IPv6 traffic passes through controlled layer-2 devices.

sections.title: The Rogue Advertisement Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 devices on a shared layer-2 segment use Router Advertisements (RAs) to announce router information. An unauthorized or incorrectly configured router can send a rogue RA, causing operational problems for other devices.

RFC 6105 describes a framework in which layer-2 switches identify invalid RAs and block them. The checks can range from a static rule about which port may send RAs to dynamic validation using Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND).
sections.plainLanguage: A rogue router can send announcements that affect other devices on the same network segment. RA-Guard places checks in the layer-2 devices that forward those announcements.

sections.title: Where RA-Guard Applies
sections.content:
RA-Guard applies when all messages between IPv6 devices pass through controlled layer-2 networking devices. It cannot protect a shared medium where devices communicate directly without passing through those devices.

The RFC presents RA-Guard as a complement to SEND, not a replacement. A switch can authorize routers on behalf of hosts, including by checking SEND certificates, so every host does not need to perform the same check.
sections.plainLanguage: RA-Guard can check announcements for hosts only when their traffic passes through the checking device. It can work alongside SEND when devices do not all support SEND themselves.

sections.title: Stateless Filtering Rules
sections.content:
Stateless RA-Guard decides whether to forward an RA using the message and the switch's configuration. The device can check the sender's link-layer address, incoming port, IP source address, prefix list, or router priority.

For example, an operator can configure one switch port as router-facing. That port forwards RAs, while the other ports block them. If an RA does not match the configured rules, the device drops it.
sections.plainLanguage: A stateless device checks each announcement against its configured rules. It forwards matching announcements and drops the rest.

sections.title: Learning and Forwarding States
sections.content:
Stateful RA-Guard learns which connected devices send valid RAs and remembers that information. In discovery-based operation, it has four states: OFF, LEARNING, BLOCKING, and FORWARDING. During LEARNING, the device gathers information for a configured period or after a triggering event.

After learning, an interface moves to BLOCKING if no valid router was found, or FORWARDING if one was found. An operator or a triggered event can move an interface between these states. In SEND-based operation, the state machine is per-peer and follows RFC 3971.
sections.plainLanguage: In learning mode, the device identifies valid router ports. It then blocks announcements on other ports and forwards valid ones on the learned ports.

sections.title: SEND Validation and Limitations
sections.content:
In SEND-based RA-Guard, the layer-2 device checks a Cryptographically Generated Address and RSA signature. It then uses a cached certificate or requests and validates a certificate chain; if validation fails, it drops the RA. The device should have a trust-anchor certificate.

RA-Guard does not protect IPv6 traffic that is tunneled or that bypasses controlled layer-2 devices. The RFC also says operators should enter LEARNING intentionally and check that the learned router list matches the expected list.
sections.plainLanguage: SEND-based filtering checks the router's cryptographic proof before forwarding an announcement. The protection fails if traffic can avoid the checking device, so operators must also verify what the device learns.
